Prevention: Before irrigation, check the soil moisture level by hand.
If soil is moist then don’t irrigate.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead irrigation to minimise the risk of the disease developing in the field.
Undertake crop rotation by using different plant families, especially root vegetables like onions, carrots and radish.
If you enter a wet, infected field, wash clothing before entering an uninfected field to avoid transporting the disease.
Avoid growing cucumber in the field where cucurbits have been planted the previous 2 years.
Monitoring: This is a bacterial disease that proliferates in warm, moist weather.
Wind and rain transmit the bacterial disease to plants, as well as workers moving through the field.
Observe crops weekly, notably on leaves and fruit.
Look for round brown spots on the leaves.
Water-soaked spots will dry out and turn yellow-brown.
Symptoms may appear on fruit during later stages of disease spread.
Infected plants will grow poorly, resulting in poorly developed fruit.
Action is required as soon as the disease is detected on crops.
If you see irregularly shaped holes in the leaves of several plants, direct control is too late and you must focus on prevention of future infections.
Direct Control (Chemical): Usually at 2 g/L, double-check product label. 7-10 days interval
Restrictions: No chemical pesticide can cure the crop of the bacterial disease.
If you know the disease to occur in neighbouring fields and if it is still not in your field and no symptoms seen
then you can try a protective spray.
When using a pesticide or botanical, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
Always consult recent list of registered pesticides.
II moderately acute hazardous to humans.
Usually at 3 g/L, check product label.
II moderately hazardous. 1 spray at the beginning of the disease.
